title: Setting Up Sparkling Water Simulation in Houdini
author: Max Schwugier (ManvsMachine), interview by 80 Level
trick: A photoreal glass of sparkling water without FLIP: the liquid top is a mesh driven by a ripple solver, and the fizz is three separate particle systems. (1) In-liquid bubbles spawn on the bottom at noise-field-driven locations, pscale grows with age so they swell as they rise, and they die on touching the surface. (2) Surface spritz gets an upward velocity only while young, then gravity pulls it back and it dies on the surface. (3) Rim bubbles spawn on a falloff at the glass edge, barely move, grow with age, then die. Bubbles and water are fused with VDBs so the surface bubbles up where they meet it; caustics follow Ross Mason's method; Redshift at about 15 min a frame on a 3090.
why: A ManvsMachine designer's own breakdown of exactly our shot (a still glass of fizzing water), with the full bubble-lifecycle logic and the 'no FLIP' shortcut. Houdini terms, but every rule (spawn on the floor, size by age, kill at the surface, rim bubbles, surface spritz) maps one to one onto Blender Geometry Nodes simulation zones.

title: Bud Light Seltzer - Truckin' Bubbles (VFX breakdown)
author: PrePost
trick: Seltzer-bubble look-dev from macro reference: shade bubbles as air pockets (the image behind is not flipped), not as liquid-filled spheres (flipped); give every bubble a shell thickness after the sim so the refraction is right, plus slight normal noise for warping. The motion R&D was the balance of 'wobble' and of large hero bubbles against nucleation sites. Pick the method per shot by how much art direction it needs: Vellum sims, C4D soft bodies with X-Particles, or plain spheres with an animated displacement map.
why: A studio breakdown of a national seltzer campaign with the concrete shading decision (air pocket = no image flip) that makes CG carbonation read as real; the rule carries straight to Cycles. The page blocks yt-rag's fetcher (HTTP 403), so the faithful text is saved as text_file.

title: The fluid mechanics of bubbly drinks
author: Roberto Zenit and Javier Rodríguez-Rodríguez (Physics Today)
trick: How real carbonation behaves, to drive a believable fizz: bubbles are born at nucleation sites (gas pockets pinned in wall crevices or trapped in fibres) and detach in regular trails, leaving a cavity that repeats the cycle. While rising, a bubble's radius grows at a constant rate (tenths of a mm per second), so bubbles visibly inflate and speed up as they rise; this is not caused by pressure change. Many trails drive a global circulation in the glass, faster near the walls. At the surface a bubble either bursts within milliseconds (pure liquid) or floats (surfactants); the burst leaves a cavity that shoots a jet and tiny aerosol droplets; when production outpaces bursting, a foam head forms.
why: Older than the 2022 bar, but it is the authoritative account of the exact behaviours the agent had to invent (nucleation streams, growth and acceleration while rising, surface pops, circulation), and nothing newer explains them as precisely. It turns the agent's guessed numbers into physics-backed rules.

title: Simulating Sparkling Liquid Pouring Into A Glass With Houdini
author: Sergey Kharitonov (via 80 Level)
trick: Render a sparkling drink with nested dielectrics instead of booleans or shrinking the liquid: glass IOR 1.5 at priority 0 (highest), air bubbles IOR 1.0 at priority 5, liquid IOR 1.33 at priority 10 (lowest), set on the Render Geometry Settings or Karma Material Properties node. Where volumes overlap only the highest-priority shader renders, which acts as a render-time boolean, so liquid may overlap the glass and bubbles may sit inside the liquid.
why: Short (about 2.3k chars) but exact: the glass, bubble and liquid IOR and priority stack for a carbonated drink. Karma has the priority feature and Cycles does not, so pair it with Christopher 3D's Blender workaround (relative IOR at each interface); the bubble-as-air rule (IOR 1.0 inside liquid) carries over directly.

title: Simulation Nodes Tutorial: Bubbles Generator | Blender 3.6 Geometry Nodes
author: MTR Animation
trick: A rising-bubble emitter in a Geometry Nodes simulation zone: a velocity vector is stored as simulation state, and each frame Join Geometry adds a fresh Distribute Points batch with a new seed. A captured Random Value gives each batch its own rise speed (randomness must be captured inside the sim or it re-rolls every frame). A normalized Noise Texture adds XY wander only, never Z, and the instance scale is randomized and tied to the speed range. The source is an icosphere that follows an Empty, so you can place one per nucleation site.
why: The Blender GN bubble recipe the agent could not find (it improvised one from a glass-particles skeleton): sim-zone state, per-batch random speed, wobble via noise, size variation. Place one emitter per nucleation site and add growth by age to get the reference's bubble streams.

title: Careful! - EXTREME Bubbles - Blender Geometry Nodes
author: Default Cube
trick: Fully procedural bubble streams in Geometry Nodes, with no point-distribute node: the points are spawned with raw maths along any curve and flow along its arc. A per-point random value drives the travel factor, which is animated and divided to set flow speed, and Vector Rotate spreads the points outward around the curve normal. Separate controls set density, bubble size, flow and rotation; the stream follows whatever curve you plug in (straight, arc, spiral).
why: Niche advanced (about 23k views) from a top Geometry Nodes educator, who used it on a commercial and suggests it for drink spots. A curve per nucleation site gives art-directable bubble strings rising from the glass floor, the walls and the undersides of ice, which a volume scatter cannot do.

title: Blender Glass and Liquid Animation Tutorial
author: Polygon Runway
trick: A looping lemonade glass, built end to end. The liquid top is displaced by a texture whose coordinates follow an Empty animated through a full cycle, so it loops. Ice cubes float with a Shrink Wrap constraint to the liquid surface (location only) plus their own rotation. Bubbles are an object-instanced particle system with gravity off, velocity 0.1 m/s and a 60-frame lifetime. For a seamless loop, a duplicate particle system starts at frame -360 and both are baked, so frames 1 and 360 hold the same bubbles. Shading covers the glass and liquid materials and lighting.
why: Solid production walkthrough (77k views, about 4% likes) covering three of our gaps in one Blender scene: bubbles, ice floating on a moving surface, and the seamless-loop maths the agent marked as its own invention.

title: Guest Tutorial: Adding Bubbles to your FLIP Simulation
author: Entagma (guest tutorial)
trick: Make bubbles from a liquid sim's own points. Keep a random 3–10 % of points by thresholding rand(@id) and copy spheres onto them. Randomize pscale with the stable ID attribute as seed, never the point number, which changes every frame and makes bubble sizes flicker. With receding (or constant emission), points are born and killed mid-sim and bubbles pop in and out, so freeze the first and last frames with Time Shift and keep only IDs that persist, and for constant emission only turn points into bubbles once @age > 0.1.
why: Entagma is top tier for procedural FX and this is niche (about 4% likes). The flicker and pop-in failures it fixes are exactly what happens with Blender sim-zone or particle bubbles too: seed by a stored ID and don't let bubbles spawn or vanish mid-shot.

title: Foam | Effects of After Effects
author: Jake In Motion
trick: AE's stock Foam effect as a bubble simulator: the bubbles collide, clump, jiggle and pop. Producer point, X/Y size and orientation set the emission shape; under Bubbles, Size, Size Variance, Lifespan, Bubble Growth Speed and Strength (how likely to pop) shape the fizz. Physics controls velocity, wind, wobble and stickiness. A Flow Map steers the bubbles along a luma image, and Rendered mode uses your own bubble texture layer.
why: The only stock-AE bubble sim with growth, collision and popping built in, explained control by control by a top AE educator. It fills the 'no AE fizz route' gap for overlays or a surface-pop layer comped over a Blender plate.

title: Shoot Clear-Liquid Bottle Photography Like a Pro!
author: Karl Taylor (Visual Education)
trick: Light clear liquid from behind. A single bare bulb through a frosted acrylic panel makes a glow that falls off toward the edges, and that vignette is what draws the bottle's dark refracted contours and the luminous liquid. Put the product on polished metal instead of a mirror: a single-surface reflection with no double image when shooting low. Use a 100–150 mm lens, centred and low for an imposing look, at f/16. Do condensation with glycerin droplets: flattened beads look more real than round ones and don't run or evaporate under lights.
why: A top product-photography educator lighting exactly a clear liquid in glass. The gradient-backlight principle maps directly to a Blender area light with a radial-gradient texture behind the glass, which is what makes CG liquid glow instead of looking grey.

title: How We Shot These 5 Cocktails | Food Lighting Tips
author: Syrp Lab
trick: Five drink lighting styles, each built light by light. Motel style: one high, distant Fresnel for a single long, crisp glass shadow, a second Fresnel shining through the cloudy drink for a warm glow, a rim light that just catches the ice top for sparkle, and a separate background Fresnel for a radial gradient. Magazine style: soft key from the side, a background light pulled far back (inverse-square law) for an even gradient, f/13 for front-to-back sharpness. Sci-fi style: black background, backlight through the drink, and new scratch-free black perspex for the reflection directly below.
why: Compact and concrete (171k views, 3.7% likes): each look is a recipe of light positions and purposes for a liquid in glass, so the agent can choose a drink-lighting style and rebuild it with Blender lights.

title: How to Professionally Light and Create a Whiskey Commercial
author: Austen Paul
trick: Light a glass bottle for a commercial, one light at a time. Raise the product on a small black box so lights can come close and the highlights stay controlled, with black duvetyne under it to kill table reflections. Shoot a 100 mm macro slightly below the product for a heroic look. Key high and slightly forward through vertical diffusion, so a clean ribbon highlight runs the full height of the bottle. Put the second light behind and angle it away, which makes the edge sliver thinner and keeps the contour; keep it dimmer than the key for contrast.
why: A working commercial DP's real job, with the reasoning for each light (ribbon highlight, thin edge sliver, contrast). It is the glass-bottle highlight language a Blender drink render needs to copy.

title: Beverage Commercial Production: Inside an LA Studio Building Liquid Hero Shots at 300fps
author: BestBoy Media
trick: The beverage director's playbook. There are four canonical shots: hero pour (slow arc, low-front to side, liquid in a backlight halo), splash (energy only), condensation reveal (macro, f/8–f/11, light from behind the droplets), and open. Use slow motion only when it serves the brand. Glass lighting rule: the light belongs around the glass, not on it. Side light makes the halo, back light makes the contents glow from within, front fill is almost never used, and black flags on both sides carve the dark contour. A black sweep beats white, and motion control is used to repeat moves for passes.
why: Current (2026), written by a beverage tabletop studio, and the only source that names how drink spots move as well as how they are lit. It gives the agent a shot grammar and a lighting rule set for a living-drink shot.

title: Selters Liquid FX (case study: high-speed cinematography, motion control, practical FX)
author: fokusmedien (dir. Sören Weingarten)
trick: Shot-by-shot practical tricks from an award-winning mineral-water film. Bubbles only rise, so film them from above with a probe lens, after a 2 s air burst clears the dust. A bottle on a pneumatic piston is slammed down and pulled up to trigger maximum fizz at the exact moment. Water poured over a crystal, rotated 180° in post, gives a weightless upward flow. Floating droplets are bounced on a subwoofer. The 800 fps pour uses Phantom plus a Cinebot motion-control rig. Overexposing the water makes it glow 'pure'. Moco camera data syncs real water with a CG background.
why: A real sparkling-water campaign (2025 Platinum awards) whose choices translate into CG direction: flip a downward pour to read as weightless, slow fizz bursts, overexposed glowing water. yt-rag's fetcher misses the collapsed shot logs, so the full faithful text is saved as text_file. Its 'AI' step is frame interpolation, not AI video generation.

title: Animated Condensation Using Cinema 4D
author: Lukas Thorup
trick: Procedural condensation on a can. Static droplets are about 10k cloned 1 cm spheres squashed to 0.65 in Z, scattered on a hidden copy of the surface. A Random effector randomizes scale only, and shader and plane effectors thin and size them by region. Running droplets are clones on Tracer splines: an animated plane effector pushes them down the can, and a displacer bends the trails so they wander.
why: A top product-render educator (86k views, about 4% likes) on the detail that sells 'ice-cold drink'. The same structure works in Blender: scatter on surface, squash the instances, randomize scale by region, add a running-drop layer.

title: Photorealistic beer condensation in 3D
author: Rüdiger Lauktien (Lauktien.Studio)
trick: Condensation that reads as real, built in Blender Geometry Nodes from observed physics. Use three droplet scales: large drops, medium drops, and a micro mist. Each large drop casts a proximity field that keeps smaller drops away, giving the natural dry halo. Layered noise breaks uniformity, running streams follow the bottle curvature and clear paths through the droplet field, and the glass colour under each drop changes its refraction.
why: A Blender studio's breakdown of the rules that separate fake dot-scatter condensation from real. It complements Thorup's C4D build with the dry-halo and three-scale logic. Some marketing text, but the method section is concrete.

title: How to Animate Floating Objects (Blender Tutorial)
author: Ryan King Art
trick: A buoyancy rig for any animated liquid surface. A small proxy plane with a Shrinkwrap modifier rides the animated water (here an Ocean modifier with its time keyed linearly). The floater takes Copy Location to a vertex group holding all the proxy's vertices, so it follows the surface height. A Copy Rotation constraint to the proxy makes it tilt with the local slope. Offset Z sets how deep it sits.
why: The agent found no bobbing or buoyancy recipe and hand-keyed amplitudes. This rig makes lotus flowers, leaves and ice follow the real ripple and bump surface automatically, tilt included, so the floating motion stays physically tied to the liquid.

title: Nested Dielectrics, the key to better fluid filled objects.
author: Christopher 3D
trick: Glass and liquid in Cycles, done right. Cycles treats every IOR as relative to air, so liquid in a glass refracts wrongly. Each interface needs a relative IOR = IOR of the medium entered / IOR of the medium left. For water against glass that is 1.33/1.52 = 0.875; the full chain would be 1.52, then 0.875, then 1.14, then 0.658 back to air. Geometry options compared: the common 'liquid pushed slightly into the glass' overlap is plausible but breaks total internal reflection and won't take a relative IOR; an inward gap is wrong. The preferred 'removed section' deletes the inner glass wall where the liquid sits, so the liquid surface is the interface and takes the relative IOR. Shown in Blender 4.3.
why: The exact Cycles nested-glass recipe the library lacked; the agent had translated Redshift rules and used an overlap that this video shows breaks. Manual captions and a 7.6% like ratio: niche, advanced and precise.

title: How to get Realistic Caustics in Blender 3D
author: Kaizen
trick: Cycles shadow caustics (MNEE, Blender 3.2+) on a modelled drinking glass. Model a 64-sided glass with bevels, a thick base and a rounded rim, shaded smooth with Auto Smooth normals. Then three switches are all required: enable Shadow Caustics on the light, Cast Shadow Caustics on the glass object, and Receive Shadow Caustics on the floor. With any one missing you get nothing. Light size and position are then tuned for sharp caustics.
why: The Blender-native caustic setup the agent wrote from memory (search 26 found only Redshift), shown on the same subject, a drinking glass on a surface, with the easy-to-miss three-flag requirement.

title: Discovering Fake Caustics in Blender
author: Polyfjord
trick: Fast, animatable fake caustics. Make the pattern from two 4D Voronoi textures (Smooth F1) mixed with Difference, with a shared smoothness value and a small Add offset on one of them; then a B-spline ColorRamp for crisp contrast. Scale, randomness and the W 'evolution' are exposed as controls. Project the texture from a Spot light: its node tree uses Texture Coordinate Normal, so the pattern is cast onto the floor and anything under the light, and animating W makes the caustics crawl.
why: From 2021, just before the date bar, but it is the canonical, hugely liked technique for the agent's planned fallback (a caustic-texture light, step F5 risk). It renders noise-free in a fraction of MNEE's time and survives nested glass and liquid, where MNEE often fails.

title: Change Your Lighting Without Re-Rendering | Blender Light Groups Tutorial
author: CG Boost
trick: Blender Light Groups. Create groups in View Layer properties, then assign each light (and the World, under World > Settings) to a group. Each group renders as its own pass. Adding the group passes back together with Mix (Add) nodes rebuilds the original render, and from there each group can be brightened, dimmed, tinted or multiplied to relight the shot after rendering. The same passes go to AE in a multilayer EXR.
why: The library only had Redshift light groups and the agent had to guess the Blender setup (step F6). It is the base of the plan to art-direct the moving light play in AE without re-rendering a glass-and-caustics scene.

title: Procedural Ice Material (Blender Tutorial)
author: Ryan King Art
trick: Clear but frosty procedural ice in Cycles. Use Principled transmission 1 at IOR 1.31, with a noise texture through a ColorRamp into roughness so parts are clear and parts frosted; contrast on the ramp sets how much you can see through. A second noise goes through a ColorRamp into a Bump node, so only some patches are bumpy, like melted surface irregularities. Notes cover when roughness makes the texture look wrong and when to keep base roughness at 0.
why: The agent found no ice material at all (search 36) and wrote IOR 1.31 and frosted core from memory. This is the well-liked Blender build of exactly that, so ice reads differently from the glass it floats in.

title: Create a 3D Scene from a Single Photo in After Effects | In-Depth PARALLAX Tutorial
author: MDMZ
trick: Turn one photo into a 3D parallax scene. In Photoshop, slice the image into depth layers with pen-tool masks (shadows stay on the ground layer) and rebuild what was hidden behind each one with Content-Aware Fill, so no holes appear when the camera moves. In AE, make the layers 3D, spread them in Z, scale them back up to fill the frame, and move a 50 mm camera slowly through them. Finish with a shadow layer in Soft Light, a sunlight flare and a slight Gaussian blur (10 at most) on the distant layers for depth.
why: The canonical, most-watched still-to-3D tutorial (11.7M views; 2021, just before the bar). It covers the step the agent said was missing: cutting a single still into layers and cleaning the plates.

title: Easy Camera Projection in Blender 3d: Full VFX Tutorial
author: LightArchitect
trick: Camera projection of a photo in Blender. Set the photo as the camera background, match the perspective, then block the scene with rough planes and deformed geometry. With all vertices selected, UV > Project from View in the camera, and give it an Emission material using the photo. The projection holds only near the original camera, so keep moves small and push-ins short; it suits mid and far depth, and the seam goes where foreground elements cover it.
why: Fills the 'camera projection is absent' gap (search 24) with the Blender route. It lets the agent keep a reference still's exact look and still get real parallax and a dolly move, with the limits stated plainly.

title: Tech Talks: Creating 3D Illusions from 2D Images: Depth Maps in Adobe After Effects
author: Matt Dombrowski
trick: 2.5D motion from a single still with no plugins. Generate a depth map with Photoshop's Neural Filters > Depth Blur (Output Depth Map Only) and invert it so near is white. In AE, feed it to Displacement Map on the photo and animate the shift, which gives a parallax pan or dolly on one image. Tune the map's contrast and blur to keep edges from tearing.
why: The depth-map parallax route the agent searched for (search 2) and didn't find, using stock AE plus Photoshop's built-in depth estimation. It is cheaper than camera projection for subtle 'breathing' moves on a still.

title: Wave World + Caustics | Effects of After Effects
author: Jake In Motion
trick: AE's stock water pair. Wave World simulates ripples from animated Producers and renders a height map; set it to Height Map view on its own solid. Caustics then takes the bottom layer (the pool or image) and uses that Wave World layer as the Water Surface, producing refraction, surface colour, opacity and moving caustic light. The video covers dialing waves (grid resolution, damping, reflection of edges, pre-roll), animating producers for drops and ripples, and the ground and sky settings.
why: The library had no documentation of Wave World or Caustics (search 7). This top-educator walkthrough is the stock-AE way to put moving refraction and caustic light over a still or a render: a breathing liquid surface, or caustic play on the floor.

title: Simulation effects (Caustics, Wave World, Foam, CC Particle World, Card Dance, Shatter...)
author: Adobe Help Center
trick: Adobe's reference for every Simulation effect, property by property: Caustics (Bottom, Water with Surface/Height/Smoothing/Refractive Index, Sky, Lighting, Material, caustic Strength), Wave World (producers, grid, damping, pre-roll), Foam (Producer, Bubbles size, variance, lifespan, growth, strength, Physics, Flow Map, Rendering), plus CC Particle World and the others.
why: Exact control names and meanings for the stock water and bubble effects the library was missing. It is the reference to sit beside Jake In Motion's two walkthroughs.
